summary.text: Axial precession is a slow, continuous, gravity-driven change in the direction a spinning body's axis points, much like the wobble of a spinning top.
Earth's axis traces out a cone over a cycle of roughly 26,000 years, so the star sitting over the north celestial pole slowly changes.
Because of it, the year of the seasons is about 20 minutes shorter than the year measured by the Sun's place against the stars.

facts.label: Cycle length
facts.value: About 26,000 years for one full circuit

facts.label: Main driver
facts.value: Moon and Sun pulling on Earth's equatorial bulge

facts.label: Credited discoverer
facts.value: Hipparchus, a Greek astronomer of the 2nd century BC

facts.label: Drift rate
facts.value: About 50 arcseconds a year, 1 degree per 72 years

items.prompt: Polaris sits almost exactly over Earth's North Pole in the night sky today. What happens to its special role over many thousands of years?

options.label: It keeps the role forever, because the axis never moves
The axis slowly swings, so other stars take over the role
It loses the role only when Earth's orbit grows more oval
It burns out, forcing astronomers to pick a replacement

items.explain: The celestial poles move in large circles against the stars as the axis precesses, so different stars become the north star over time.

items.prompt: Roughly how long does Earth's axis take to sweep out one complete circle of its wobble?

options.label: About 1 year
About 260 years
About 26,000 years
About 26 million years

items.explain: Earth's precession cycle lasts approximately 26,000 years.

items.prompt: A tipped toy top slowly swings its axis around in a circle while it spins. Earth's axis does something similar. What drives Earth's version?

options.label: The Moon and Sun tugging on Earth's bulging middle
Earth's magnetic field slowly flipping north and south
Strong winds pushing against the tallest mountains
Heat leaking unevenly out of the planet's core

items.explain: The main part of the motion comes from the gravity of the Moon and Sun acting on Earth's equatorial bulge.

items.prompt: Two ways to measure a year: from one solstice to the next, or until the Sun returns to the same spot against the stars. How do they compare?

options.label: The star-based year is the shorter one
They always match to the second
Which is shorter flips every few centuries
The solstice-based year is the shorter one

items.explain: Because of precession, the seasons come round about 20 minutes before the Sun returns to the same place among the stars, so the tropical year is shorter.

items.prompt: Earth's precession used to be called the 'precession of the equinoxes'. Where does that old name come from?

options.label: The equinox points slowly crept west against the fixed stars
Astronomers thought the equinoxes pushed Earth's axis around
The wobble could only be measured on the two equinox days
Day and night at the equinoxes slowly stop being equal

items.explain: The equinoxes moved westward along the ecliptic relative to the fixed stars, so the motion was named after them.

items.prompt: Over the centuries the stars seem to shift slowly relative to the equinox points. What is mostly going on?

options.label: The stars are racing across the galaxy at great speed
Earth's orbit is steadily shrinking toward the Sun
Earth's axis is shifting, so the drift is only apparent
Starlight bends more and more as it travels to Earth

items.explain: Much of the drift is apparent: it comes from viewing the sky from Earth's slowly moving axis, not from the stars moving.
